Title: Comparison of unstructured kinetic bacterial growth models. $ ^{\star} $

Abstract: Bacteria in biological wastewater treatment process play an important role in the removal of substrate concentration. When bacteria removes the substrate, they continuously growth until such time when the substrate concentration is depleted. This paper aims to review the performance of kinetic growth rate models that describe specific bacteria growth rate. The kinetic growth rate models reviewed were: Monod, Blackman, Haldane, Teissier, Moser, Contois, Logarithmic, Powell, Han and Levenspiel, Logistic, Luong, Webb, Yano and Koga, and Aiba-Edwards. The performance review of the models were based on coefficient of determination ( $ R^{2} $). Another statistical measure of performance was root mean square error (RMSE). All kinetic growth rate models performed well when subjected to both toxic and non-toxic substrate concentration. The most notable kinetic growth rate model was the Haldane model which was well represented in the literature.

Sentences about the process and the data:
- When bacteria removes the substrate, they continuously growth until such time when the substrate concentration is depleted.
- In the lag phase, bacteria take time to acclimatize to their new environment in the bioreactor.
- While the acclimatizing process takes place, there is no growth of bacteria in the bioreactor.
- During this phase, the bacteria present in the bioreactor doubles at a high rate.
- The cell dry weight mass method has the advantage of providing direct unconditional estimates.
- In other words, cell dry weight mass method for each culture is required at least once when using the OD method.
- Unstructured kinetic growth models are more suitable for steady state balance while structured models are more suitable for unsteady state balance (Panikov, 2009).
- Description $\mu = \text{Specific growth rate } \mu_{max} = \text{Maximum Specific growth rate } S = \text{Substrate concentration } X = \text{Biomass concentration } K_{s} = \text{Half saturation constant } K_{i} = \text{Inhibition constan
- Residuals are a measure of how far from the regression line data points are (Sharifahmadian, 2015) Chai and Draxler (2014).
- The parameter constants of all the kinetic growth models are estimated using nonlinear least of squares.
- The Monod model was first introduced by Jacques Monod in 1942 to describe the relationship between specific growth rate and substrate utilization rate in a bioreactor (Monod, 1949).
- The Monod model assumes that there is only one growth limiting substrate in the bioreactor (Monod, 1942).
- Hamitouche et al., (2012) reported a poor fit on biodegradation of phenol by mixed culture in a batch reactor.
- Ardestani and Kasebkar (2018) reported a poor fit on Aspergillus niger growth and substrate uptake in a batch submerged culture.
- Ardestani and Shafiei (2014) reported a satisfactory fit on the cell growth of Saccharomyces cerevisiae in a batch culture.
- Dey and Mukherjee (2010) reported a satisfactory fit on Phenol biodegradation by mixed microbial culture in a batch reactor.
- Just like the Monod model, the Blackman model is unable to capture the lag and death phase, and in turn it over estimates the specific growth rate (Kong, 2017).
- In the study the Blackman model was the only model that did not fit the experimental data with a reported  $ R^{2} $ of 43.3%.

Model: free-floating laws (no Sup)
Laws:
(3) [constitutive] Specific bacteria growth rate as a saturating function of substrate concentration.
(4) [constitutive] Specific growth rate computed from substrate and biomass concentrations using the printed Monod-form expression.
(5) [constitutive] Specific growth rate proportional to substrate concentration in the printed expression, while the text describes substrate-independent growth at high substrate concentration.
(6) [constitutive] Specific growth rate as a function of substrate concentration with an inhibition term for toxic-substrate effects.
(7) [constitutive] Specific growth rate given by an exponential relation to substrate concentration.
(8) [constitutive] Specific growth rate as a substrate-dependent Monod extension with an adjustable exponent.
(9) [constitutive] Specific growth rate as a function of substrate and biomass concentrations in the Contois model.
(10) [constitutive] Specific growth rate as a function of the logarithm of substrate concentration.
(11) [constitutive] The Aiba–Edward law computes specific growth rate from substrate saturation with exponential suppression at high substrate concentration.
(12) [constitutive] The Yano–Koga law computes specific growth rate with substrate inhibition at high substrate concentration.
(13) [constitutive] The Han–Levenspiel law computes specific growth rate with inhibition that depends on substrate concentration and a critical inhibitor concentration.
(14) [constitutive] The Powell law computes specific growth rate from substrate saturation with an adjustment for maintenance.
(15) [constitutive] The Logistic law computes specific growth rate from biomass relative to its maximum concentration.
(16) [constitutive] The Luong law computes specific growth rate from substrate saturation with inhibition tied to a critical substrate concentration.
(17) [constitutive] The Webb law computes specific growth rate with a substrate-inhibition term in the numerator.

answer.description: The review compares unstructured kinetic laws for specific bacterial growth on substrate in biological wastewater treatment. The laws predict specific growth rate from substrate concentration, with some also depending on biomass, and represent saturation, substrate inhibition, biomass limitation, maintenance, and other empirical substrate responses. Model performance is assessed using R² and RMSE, with parameters estimated by nonlinear least squares; no particular process operating mode or fitting dataset is specified.
